anchor: the topmen, who as such had been picked out for youth and activity
note: Topmen: sailors stationed aloft, chosen for youth and agility because they worked highest on the masts.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Topmen”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Constituted: formed. The topmen are pictured as a club of idlers high in the air.

anchor: smaller stun’sails rolled up into cushions
note: Stun’sails: studding-sails, extra narrow sails set beside the main sails in light winds.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Studding-sails”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: spinning yarns like the lazy gods
note: To spin a yarn is to tell a long story, a sailors’ pastime, like idle gods.
Punctiliousness: strict attention to the exact rules of duty.
Alacrity: quick, eager readiness to act.

anchor: the first formal gangway-punishment he had ever witnessed
note: A sailor was flogged at the gangway with a whip of knotted cords while the crew watched.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Gangway”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: an afterguardsman absent from his assigned post
note: Afterguardsmen were sailors stationed on the after part of the ship, usually less skilled men.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “After-guard”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: when the ship was being put about
note: To put about is to turn the ship onto the opposite tack, a manoeuvre needing the whole crew.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Put about”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: a dereliction resulting in a rather serious hitch
note: Dereliction: neglect of duty, here leaving his post.

anchor: instantaneous promptitude in letting go and making fast
note: Promptitude: quickness. Letting go and making fast means casting off one rope and securing another.

anchor: the culprit’s naked back under the scourge
note: Scourge: a whip used to punish.
Gridironed: marked in crossing stripes like the bars of a gridiron. Welts: raised marks left by blows.
Remissness: carelessness in doing one’s duty.
Visitation: here, a dreadful experience sent as punishment.
Stowage: the way things are packed away.

anchor: a vague threat from one of them
note: One of the ship’s corporals, Claggart’s underlings, has warned Billy.
Incredulous: unwilling to believe him, almost mocking.
Bully: here a friendly word for a good fellow, as in “bully for you.”

anchor: a veteran aboard who because his years began to disqualify him
note: Veteran: someone with long experience, here an old sailor.
Mainmast-man: an older sailor stationed to look after the ropes at the foot of the mainmast.
Belayed: made fast, tied off.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Belay”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: an old Dansker long anglicized in the service
note: Dansker: a Dane. Anglicized means he has become like an Englishman.

anchor: peppered blue by the chance explosion of a gun-cartridge
note: Specks of gunpowder driven into his skin by an explosion left blue marks.
H.M.S. Agamemnon was a 64-gun ship that Nelson commanded from 1793. Men who had served under him were proud of it.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: seen a grand skeleton in Haydon’s etching
note: Etching: a print made from a metal plate. Haydon’s print shows the stripped hulk of the old ship.
A boarding party attacks an enemy ship by climbing aboard with weapons.
Athwart: across. Visage: face. The scar crosses his dark face.
Weasel-eyes: narrow, sharp little eyes like a weasel’s.
Sapience: wisdom, here a rough and old-fashioned kind.
Merlin is the wise old magician of the King Arthur legends. The Dansker, like Merlin, seems to see the future.
Quizzing: teasing, looking at someone with amusement.

anchor: a world not without some man-traps
note: Man-traps: snares set for unwary people.

anchor: simple courage, lacking experience and address
note: Address: skill and tact in handling situations.
Ascetic: living simply and severely, avoiding comfort.

anchor: eccentricities, sometimes bordering on the ursine
note: Ursine: bearlike, gruff and shaggy.

anchor: revering him as a salt hero
note: Salt: a sailor, especially an old and seasoned one.

anchor: a salutation marked by that respect
note: Salutation: a greeting, here a respectful nod each time.
Vein: a streak of something running through a person.
Patriarchal: like an old father or head of a clan.

anchor: some other and more recondite reason
note: Recondite: obscure, hard to understand.
The Dansker calls Billy “Baby,” the name that later sticks to him.
Ruminating: thinking deeply, chewing over thoughts like a cow chews cud.

anchor: seated on a shot-box of the upper gun deck
note: A shot-box held cannonballs near a gun.

anchor: surveying with a somewhat cynical regard
note: Cynical: doubting that people act from good motives.
Swaggering: walking with a proud, show-off strut.

anchor: shoving up the front of his tarpaulin
note: A tarpaulin hat is a sailor’s hat of waterproofed canvas.
Laconically: using very few words.
Jimmy Legs: sailors’ nickname for the master-at-arms, who prowled the decks on police duty.
Ejaculated: exclaimed suddenly. The word then had a harmless meaning.
Reiteration: saying something again and again.
Oracular: speaking in obscure, prophetic riddles like an oracle.
Chiron was the wise centaur of Greek myth who taught young heroes, among them Achilles.
Achilles was the Greek hero of the Trojan War, famous for his strength and beauty and for his doom.

anchor: subordinated life-long to the will of superiors
note: Subordinated: placed under another’s authority.
Pithy: short and full of meaning.
